posts.description:
3-Layer Torch-Down Flat Roof Replacement

A Complete Modified Bitumen Roofing System
When a flat or low-slope roof begins leaking, developing bubbles, separating at seams, holding water, or showing widespread deterioration, repeated patching may no longer be the best long-term solution.

A complete flat roof replacement with a 3-layer torch-down modified bitumen roofing system can provide a durable, multi-layer waterproofing system designed specifically for low-slope roofing applications.

Roof Express recently completed this type of roofing system using a comprehensive approach that addresses much more than the visible surface of the roof.

From tear-off and roof-deck inspection to new flashing, waterproofing, drainage details, and the final granulated cap sheet, each component plays an important role in the performance of the completed roof.

In this article, we'll explain what a 3-layer torch-down roof is, how the system is built, why it is commonly used on flat roofs, and what homeowners should expect from a professional flat roof replacement.
What Is a 3-Layer Torch-Down Roof?
A 3-layer torch-down roof is a multi-ply modified bitumen roofing system designed for flat and low-slope roofs.

A typical three-ply assembly can include:

Layer 1 — Base Sheet

Layer 2 — Modified Bitumen Interply or Smooth Membrane

Layer 3 — Granulated Modified Bitumen Cap Sheet

GAF, for example, publishes three-ply APP modified-bitumen assemblies consisting of a base sheet, interply, and cap membrane.

Together, these layers create a reinforced roofing assembly rather than relying on a single membrane for waterproofing.

The exact products and attachment methods should always be selected according to the roof design, substrate, manufacturer requirements, applicable building codes, and project conditions.
Why Use Modified Bitumen on a Flat Roof?
Flat and low-slope roofs behave differently from steep pitched roofs.

On a steep roof, gravity moves rainwater toward the gutters relatively quickly.

On a low-slope roof, water drains more slowly. That makes waterproofing, seams, flashing, penetrations, and drainage especially important.

Modified bitumen roofing systems are specifically designed for low-slope applications. Manufacturers including CertainTeed and GAF identify modified-bitumen systems as options for residential and commercial low-slope roofing.

A properly selected multi-layer modified bitumen system can provide:

Strong waterproofing

Multiple layers of protection

Reinforced roofing membranes

Resistance to normal roof movement

Protection against sun and weather exposure

Durable seams

Protection around penetrations

A finished granulated surface

Long-term performance when correctly installed and maintained

Our Flat Roof Replacement Process
A quality flat roof replacement starts long before the final cap sheet is installed.

The condition underneath the existing roofing is equally important.

Here is how a professional 3-layer torch-down roof replacement is approached.
1. Existing Flat Roof Inspection
Before beginning the project, the existing roofing system should be carefully evaluated.

The inspection may identify problems including:

Active roof leaks

Open seams

Bubbles or blisters

Cracked roofing membranes

Ponding water

Failed flashing

Deteriorated roof edges

Damaged drain areas

Previous roofing patches

Soft roof decking

Deterioration around skylights

Problems around plumbing vents

Roof-to-wall leakage

Understanding the existing problems helps determine the appropriate replacement scope.
2. Complete Tear-Off of Existing Roofing
For a complete roof replacement, the deteriorated roofing materials are removed from the areas included in the project.

A tear-off may include removing:

Existing roofing membranes

Old cap sheets

Underlying roofing layers

Loose roofing materials

Deteriorated flashing

Damaged accessories

Roofing debris

Removing the old roof exposes the underlying deck so its condition can be evaluated.

This is one of the biggest advantages of a complete tear-off compared with simply installing another roofing layer over an unknown substrate.
3. Roof Deck Inspection
Once the existing roofing is removed, the roof deck becomes visible.

The decking is inspected for conditions such as:

Rotten plywood

Water damage

Delamination

Soft areas

Previous improper repairs

Dry rot

Damaged wood

Structural concerns

A new roofing system performs best when installed over a sound and properly prepared substrate.

Installing premium roofing over severely deteriorated decking does not correct the underlying problem.
4. Replacement of Deteriorated Roof Decking
Any roof-deck areas requiring replacement should be addressed before installing the new waterproofing system.

This may involve removing deteriorated sheathing and replacing it with suitable new roof decking.

Once repairs are completed, the contractor has a solid substrate for installation of the new roofing assembly.
5. Drainage and Ponding Evaluation
Drainage is one of the most important considerations on any flat roof.

Before installing the new roofing system, existing drainage conditions should be evaluated.

Water should be directed toward designated drainage points such as:

Roof drains

Scuppers

Gutters

Downspouts

Minor temporary water accumulation immediately following rain can occur on some low-slope roofs, but significant or persistent ponding should be evaluated.

When necessary and included in the project scope, drainage improvements may involve corrections to the substrate, tapered materials, crickets, framing, or other modifications.

The objective is not only to install new roofing but also to provide the best practical water-management system for the existing building.
6. Installation of the First Layer — Base Sheet
The first component of the new roofing assembly is the base sheet.

The base sheet creates the foundation for the modified bitumen roofing system and separates the finished membranes from the underlying roof deck or approved substrate.

The specific type of base sheet and attachment method depend on the roofing manufacturer, substrate, roof design, and selected system.

This first layer is extremely important because every additional membrane depends on the preparation underneath it.
7. Installation of the Second Layer — Modified Bitumen Interply
The second roofing layer provides another reinforced waterproofing membrane.

This layer may be referred to as the:

Interply

Ply sheet

Smooth modified bitumen membrane

Intermediate membrane

depending on the manufacturer and roofing system.

Adding an intermediate layer gives the roofing assembly additional redundancy.

Instead of depending on one finished membrane alone, a 3-ply system provides multiple layers between the building and outside weather.
8. Installation of the Third Layer — Granulated Cap Sheet
The final roofing layer is typically the granulated modified bitumen cap sheet.

The cap sheet forms the visible finished surface of the roof.

Its granulated surface helps protect the modified bitumen membrane against exposure while creating a durable finished roofing surface.

This final layer must be carefully integrated with:

Roof edges

Drains

Scuppers

Flashing

Plumbing vents

Skylights

Walls

Other roof penetrations

The performance of a flat roof depends heavily on these details.
Why Three Layers Instead of One?
One of the biggest advantages of a multi-ply roofing system is redundancy.

A 3-layer modified bitumen system does not rely solely on one membrane.

The complete assembly provides:

Base Sheet + Interply + Cap Sheet

Each layer performs a different function within the roofing system.

The result is a robust roofing assembly designed for low-slope environments where water moves more slowly than it does on a pitched roof.

Multi-ply modified-bitumen construction is recognized by roofing manufacturers as an established low-slope roofing approach.
Torch-Down Roofing and Waterproof Seams
Torch-applied modified bitumen uses heat during professional installation to bond compatible membrane layers together.

When installed according to the roofing manufacturer's specifications, the process creates tightly bonded membrane seams designed to resist water intrusion. GAF describes torch-down installation as heating modified-bitumen membrane so it bonds to the layer beneath.

Because torch-applied roofing involves open-flame equipment and specialized procedures, installation should be handled by trained roofing professionals following manufacturer requirements and appropriate fire-safety procedures.
Flashing Is Just as Important as the Roofing Membrane
A flat roof can contain excellent roofing material and still leak if the flashing details are poorly installed.

Many roof leaks begin at transitions rather than in the middle of the membrane.

Important areas include:

Roof-to-wall connections

Parapet walls

Skylights

Chimneys

Plumbing vents

Roof drains

Scuppers

HVAC penetrations

Electrical penetrations

Roof edges

Transitions between flat and pitched roofs

These areas require careful waterproofing and integration with the new roofing system.
Roof Drains and Scuppers
Water management is especially important on a flat roof.

Drain and scupper areas should be inspected as part of the reroofing process.

Common drainage problems include:

Clogged drains

Deteriorated drain flashing

Damaged drain components

Improper slope toward the drain

Debris accumulation

Water backing up at walls

Undersized or poorly located drainage points

A beautiful new roofing membrane will not perform at its best if the drainage system is ignored.
Skylights on Flat Roofs
Many flat roofs contain skylights.

These can become common leak locations when old flashing, deteriorated curbs, sealants, or surrounding roofing begins to fail.

During a flat roof replacement, skylights should be inspected for:

Deteriorated curb framing

Rotted wood

Damaged glazing

Failed seals

Corrosion

Previous repairs

Interior moisture staining

Deteriorated flashing

If an older skylight is already near the end of its service life, replacing it during the roofing project can make sense.

This allows the new skylight and new roofing system to be integrated together from the beginning.
Flat Roof Penetrations
Every penetration through the roof creates a potential waterproofing challenge.

Common flat-roof penetrations include:

Plumbing pipes

Exhaust vents

Electrical conduits

HVAC equipment

Skylights

Roof drains

Solar equipment

Chimneys

Each penetration must be properly incorporated into the roofing and flashing system.

Applying roofing cement around an old penetration should not be considered a substitute for properly designed flashing when replacement is required.
Roof-to-Wall Connections
Roof-to-wall transitions deserve special attention.

These locations commonly experience water intrusion because runoff can become concentrated along the wall.

Depending on the structure, waterproofing may involve properly integrated flashing, membrane upturns, counterflashing, siding coordination, or other system-specific details.

The exact design depends on the building and existing construction.
Granulated Cap Sheet Finish
Once the final cap sheet is installed, the roof has a clean and uniform finished surface.

Granulated cap sheets are popular because they combine the waterproofing characteristics of modified bitumen with a protective finished surface.

Depending on the selected roofing system, different cap-sheet colors or reflective surfaces may also be available.

Product selection should be based on manufacturer requirements and any applicable energy-code requirements.
Final Roof Inspection
After the roofing installation is completed, the finished system should be carefully reviewed.

The final inspection should include checking major roofing details such as:

Membrane surface

Seams

Roof edges

Flashing

Penetrations

Drain areas

Scuppers

Skylights

Roof-to-wall transitions

Finished waterproofing details

The roof and surrounding work areas should also be cleaned of construction debris.

Where a permit is required, applicable building inspections should also be completed.
Benefits of a 3-Layer Torch-Down Flat Roof
A professionally installed 3-layer modified bitumen roofing system offers several potential benefits.
Multi-Layer Protection
Three roofing plies provide redundancy rather than relying on one membrane.
Excellent Low-Slope Application
Modified bitumen is designed for flat and low-slope roofing applications.
Strong Waterproofing
Properly installed membrane systems create continuous waterproof roofing coverage.
Reinforced Roofing
Modified bitumen membranes incorporate reinforcing materials designed to improve strength and durability.
Resistance to Normal Building Movement
Modified bitumen systems are designed to accommodate normal thermal expansion and contraction better than rigid roofing materials in appropriate applications.
Durable Finished Surface
The granulated cap sheet provides a protective finished roofing surface.
Multiple Flashing Options
The system can be professionally detailed around many common flat-roof penetrations and transitions.
Is a 3-Layer Torch-Down Roof Right for Every Building?
Not necessarily.

The correct roofing system depends on:

Roof slope

Existing roofing

Roof deck

Building occupancy

Fire-safety requirements

Drainage

Building code

Roof access

Manufacturer requirements

Nearby combustible materials

Project design

Torch-applied roofing is only one method of installing modified bitumen.

Other systems include self-adhered and other approved installation methods.

A professional roof inspection should be completed before deciding which system is most appropriate.
When Should a Flat Roof Be Replaced?
You should consider a professional roof evaluation when you notice:

Recurring leaks

Open seams

Large bubbles

Cracked membrane

Widespread deterioration

Water entering around drains

Deteriorated flashing

Significant ponding

Soft roof decking

Multiple previous patches

Interior ceiling stains

Failed skylight flashing

An aging roofing system requiring frequent repairs

Repair may still be appropriate when a problem is limited to one isolated area and the remaining roofing system is in good condition.

However, continuing to patch a roof that is failing throughout can become increasingly expensive.
Flat Roof Repair vs. Complete Replacement
A professional roofing contractor should evaluate whether repair or complete replacement makes more sense.
A Repair May Be Appropriate When:

Damage is isolated

The roofing system is relatively young

The surrounding membrane remains in good condition

A specific penetration or flashing detail has failed

Complete Replacement May Be Better When:

Leaks occur in multiple areas

Roofing membranes are deteriorating throughout

Numerous previous repairs exist

Moisture has reached the roof deck

Seams are failing in multiple locations

The roof has reached the later stages of its useful life

Repair costs continue increasing

The goal should be to solve the roofing problem, not simply cover the visible symptom.
How Long Does a 3-Layer Modified Bitumen Roof Last?
There is no single guaranteed lifespan for every flat roof.

Actual service life can depend on:

Roofing materials

Number of plies

Manufacturer

Installation quality

Roof drainage

Building movement

Sun exposure

Foot traffic

Maintenance

Penetrations

Climate

Flashing details

Regular inspections and maintenance can help identify small issues before they develop into larger roofing problems.

Homeowners should also distinguish between a manufacturer's material warranty and a roofing contractor's workmanship warranty.

They are not the same thing.
Maintaining Your New Flat Roof
Even a newly installed roofing system should be periodically inspected.

Flat-roof maintenance can include:

Keeping drains clear

Removing accumulated leaves and debris

Checking scuppers

Inspecting flashing

Checking penetrations

Monitoring skylights

Looking for membrane damage

Checking areas exposed to frequent foot traffic

Inspecting after major storms or construction work

Avoid allowing other trades to cut, drill, or place equipment directly through a new roofing membrane without proper roofing coordination.

Many flat-roof problems begin after HVAC, solar, electrical, plumbing, or other contractors disturb an existing roofing system.
Why Complete Roof Preparation Matters
The final cap sheet may be the only layer visible after the project is finished, but the quality of a roof depends heavily on everything underneath.

A complete flat roofing assembly can be thought of as:

Roof Deck → Base Sheet → Modified Bitumen Interply → Granulated Cap Sheet → Flashing → Drainage

Every component has a purpose.

That is why Roof Express focuses on the complete roofing system, not simply the visible top layer.
3-Layer Torch-Down Flat Roof Project Completed
The completed roofing system provides the property with a new multi-layer modified bitumen roof designed specifically for low-slope conditions.

The project addresses the major components required for a complete roof replacement, including preparation of the substrate, waterproofing layers, roofing membranes, penetrations, roof edges, flashing, and drainage details included within the project scope.

The final result is a clean, professionally finished flat roofing system built around multiple layers of waterproof protection.
Need a Flat Roof Replacement?
If your flat roof is leaking, deteriorating, holding water, or requiring repeated repairs, it may be time for a professional inspection.

Roof Express provides flat roof inspections, modified bitumen roof replacement, torch-down roofing, flashing repairs, skylight work, drainage corrections, roof-deck replacement, and complete low-slope roofing systems.

Our team can inspect the existing conditions and provide a detailed roofing proposal based on the needs of your property.

Contact Roof Express today to schedule your flat roof inspection and request an estimate for a 3-layer modified bitumen roofing system.
Frequently Asked Questions About 3-Layer Torch-Down RoofingWhat is a 3-layer torch-down roof?
A three-layer system typically consists of a base sheet, an intermediate modified-bitumen ply, and a finished modified-bitumen cap sheet. The exact assembly varies by roofing manufacturer and project specification.
Is torch-down roofing good for flat roofs?
Modified bitumen systems are widely used for flat and low-slope roofing applications. Whether torch application is appropriate depends on the particular building, roof conditions, safety requirements, code requirements, and manufacturer specifications.
What is modified bitumen roofing?
Modified bitumen is an asphalt-based roofing membrane modified with polymers and reinforced for use in roofing systems. APP and SBS are two common modified-bitumen technologies.
Why install three roofing layers?
A three-ply system provides multiple layers of waterproofing protection and redundancy rather than relying exclusively on one membrane.
What is the top layer of a torch-down roof?
The visible finished layer is commonly a granulated modified-bitumen cap sheet, depending on the selected roofing system.
Can a torch-down roof be installed over an existing roof?
Sometimes existing conditions allow an overlay system, but a complete roof evaluation is required. Existing roofing condition, number of layers, moisture, decking, code requirements, manufacturer specifications, and roof weight must all be considered.
What happens if rotten plywood is found?
Deteriorated decking should be addressed before installing the new roofing system so the membranes have a suitable substrate.
Can a torch-down roof fix ponding water?
Installing a new membrane does not automatically correct an existing slope or drainage problem. Significant ponding should be evaluated separately, and drainage or slope corrections may need to be included in the project scope.
Can skylights be replaced during a flat roof replacement?
Yes. Roof replacement is often a good time to replace aging skylights because the new skylight flashing and roofing system can be integrated together.
Does a torch-down roof need maintenance?
Yes. Drains should remain clear, and the roofing membrane, flashing, skylights, penetrations, and drainage areas should be inspected periodically.
How do I get an estimate for a 3-layer flat roof replacement?

Schedule a professional roof inspection with Roof Express. The existing roofing system, decking, drainage, flashing, penetrations, and access conditions can then be evaluated before a detailed proposal is prepared.

Shingle Roof Replacement in San Jose, CA
A new shingle roof can completely improve the appearance, protection, and long-term performance of your home.

Roof Express recently completed a shingle roof replacement in San Jose, California, giving the property a fresh roofing system designed to provide dependable weather protection and a clean, modern appearance.

For homeowners considering a roof replacement in San Jose, asphalt architectural shingles remain one of the most popular residential roofing choices because they combine durability, attractive design, manufacturer warranty options, and strong overall value.
Complete Removal of the Existing Roof
A quality roof replacement starts with proper preparation.

For a complete reroofing project, the existing roofing materials are removed so the roof deck underneath can be inspected.

This process may include removal and disposal of:

Existing shingles

Old roofing underlayment

Loose or deteriorated flashing

Roofing nails and fasteners

Damaged roofing accessories

Construction debris

Removing the old roof gives our roofing team the opportunity to inspect the condition underneath instead of simply covering existing problems.
Roof Deck Inspection
After tear-off, the exposed roof deck is carefully inspected.

We look for issues such as:

Rotten plywood

Water-damaged sheathing

Soft roof decking

Dry rot

Delamination

Previous improper repairs

Structural damage

A new shingle roof should always be installed over a solid and properly prepared roofing surface.

If damaged plywood is discovered, the deteriorated areas should be replaced before the new roofing system is installed.
New Roofing Underlayment
After the roof deck is prepared, new roofing underlayment is installed.

Underlayment provides an additional protective barrier between the roof deck and the finished shingles.

A complete roofing system should not rely only on the shingles visible from the street.

The roofing assembly works together as a system:

Roof Deck → Underlayment → Flashing → Shingles → Ventilation → Drainage

Each component is important to the performance of the completed roof.
Waterproofing Critical Areas
Certain parts of a roof are more vulnerable to water intrusion.

During a San Jose shingle roof replacement, special attention should be given to areas such as:

Roof valleys

Eaves

Skylights

Plumbing vents

Chimneys

Roof-to-wall connections

Roof penetrations

Proper waterproofing and flashing around these locations can help prevent future leaks.
New Architectural Shingle Installation
Once the roof deck, underlayment, and waterproofing details are prepared, the new architectural shingles are installed.

Architectural shingles are a popular choice for San Jose homeowners because they provide:

Attractive dimensional appearance

Multiple color options

Strong weather protection

Manufacturer warranty options

Good durability

Excellent value for residential homes

Modern architectural shingles also create a more premium look compared with traditional three-tab shingles.
Proper Roof Flashing
Flashing is one of the most important parts of any roofing project.

Even a premium shingle can experience leakage if surrounding flashing is not installed correctly.

Important flashing areas may include:

Plumbing vents

Skylights

Chimneys

Sidewalls

Headwalls

Roof valleys

Roof penetrations

These details should be properly integrated into the new roofing system.
Roof Ventilation
Roof replacement is also a good time to evaluate attic ventilation.

Proper ventilation can help reduce excessive heat and moisture accumulation inside the attic.

Depending on the home, ventilation may include:

Intake vents

Roof vents

Ridge ventilation

Other approved ventilation systems

The goal is to create balanced airflow through the attic where appropriate.
Cleanup and Final Inspection
Once the new roofing system is installed, the property should be thoroughly cleaned.

Our roofing cleanup process includes removing construction debris and inspecting the surrounding work area.

The completed roof is then reviewed for important details including:

Shingle alignment

Flashing

Roof penetrations

Roof edges

Ridge areas

Ventilation

Finished roofing details

The result is a clean and professionally installed new shingle roof.
Benefits of a New Shingle Roof in San Jose
Replacing an aging roof can provide several important benefits.
Better Weather Protection
A complete new roofing system helps protect the structure against rain and moisture.
Improved Curb Appeal
New architectural shingles can dramatically improve the appearance of a home.
Reduced Risk of Roof Leaks
Replacing deteriorated roofing, underlayment, and flashing can eliminate many common sources of leaks.
Opportunity to Repair Damaged Decking
A complete tear-off allows damaged plywood and concealed conditions to be identified.
Manufacturer Warranty Options
Many premium shingle systems are available with strong manufacturer warranty programs when installed according to applicable requirements.
Improved Home Value
A professionally installed new roof can make a home more attractive to potential buyers and reduce concerns about major deferred maintenance.
When Should You Replace Your Shingle Roof?
San Jose homeowners should consider having their roof inspected when they notice:

Missing shingles

Cracked shingles

Curling shingles

Significant granule loss

Repeated leaks

Interior ceiling stains

Damaged flashing

Soft roof decking

Multiple previous repairs

An aging roofing system

Not every roofing issue requires complete replacement.

A localized problem may sometimes be repaired.

However, when the roof is deteriorating throughout, a complete replacement may provide a more reliable long-term solution.
Roof Repair vs. Shingle Roof Replacement
A roof repair may be appropriate when:

Damage is limited to a small area

The roof is relatively new

Most shingles remain in good condition

One flashing or penetration is causing the problem

A complete roof replacement may make more sense when:

The roof has multiple leaks

Shingles are deteriorated throughout

Repairs have been performed repeatedly

The roofing system is approaching the end of its expected service life

Significant roof-deck damage is present

A professional roof inspection can help determine the right approach.
Choosing a Roofing Contractor in San Jose
Your roofing contractor can be just as important as the roofing product you choose.

Before hiring a roofing contractor, homeowners should ask about:

California contractor licensing

Insurance

Roofing materials

Tear-off and disposal

Roofing underlayment

Flashing

Waterproofing

Plywood replacement

Permits

Manufacturer warranties

Contractor workmanship warranties

Cleanup

Project exclusions

A detailed written roofing proposal allows homeowners to understand exactly what is included.

Professional Shingle Roof Replacement in San Jose

Roof Replacement in San Francisco, CA

Complete Homeowner Guide
A roof replacement in San Francisco requires more than simply removing old roofing material and installing a new roof.

San Francisco homes present roofing contractors with unique conditions. The city has dense neighborhoods, older Victorian and Edwardian buildings, attached properties, narrow access areas, flat and low-slope roofs, skylights, rooftop decks, chimneys, parapet walls, fog, coastal moisture, wind, and complicated roof-to-wall transitions.

Because of these factors, choosing the right roofing system — and the right San Francisco roofing contractor — can make a major difference in how your new roof performs over the years.

At Roof Express, we provide professional residential roof replacement throughout San Francisco and the surrounding Bay Area. Our goal is to evaluate the entire roofing system rather than simply covering visible problems.

In this complete guide, we'll explain when to replace your roof, what a professional reroofing project should include, roofing material options, San Francisco permit considerations, flat-roof replacement, skylights, roof decking, costs, project timelines, and how to choose a qualified roofing contractor.
When Should You Replace Your Roof in San Francisco?
A roof does not necessarily need replacement simply because it develops one leak.

Some isolated roofing problems can be successfully repaired.

However, once deterioration becomes widespread or the roofing system reaches the later stages of its service life, continuing to perform temporary repairs can become expensive and unreliable.

Common signs that you may need a roof replacement in San Francisco include:

Repeated roof leaks

Missing or damaged shingles

Cracked, curled, or deteriorated shingles

Significant granule loss

Open seams in flat roofing

Blisters or bubbles in roofing membranes

Deteriorated roof flashing

Soft or damaged plywood

Dry rot around roof penetrations

Ponding water on low-slope roofs

Water stains on ceilings or walls

Deterioration around skylights

Damaged chimney or parapet flashing

Multiple previous roof patches

Roofing approaching the end of its useful service life

Leaks appearing in several different areas

If repairs are required every rainy season, it may be time to evaluate whether replacing the entire roofing system is more practical.
Why San Francisco Roofs Are Different
San Francisco is one of the most unique roofing markets in California.

Homes located only a few blocks apart can have completely different roofing systems.

You may find:

Victorian homes with steep pitched roofs

Edwardian buildings

Multi-unit residential buildings

Flat-roof homes

Low-slope roofs

Combination pitched and flat roofing

Asphalt shingle roofs

Modified bitumen roofs

Skylights and custom skylights

Rooftop decks

Parapet walls

Closely attached neighboring roofs

A roofing contractor working in San Francisco must understand how these different components interact.
Coastal Moisture and Fog
San Francisco's climate can expose roofs to frequent fog and moisture even when it isn't raining.

Water management is therefore extremely important.

Details around flashing, drains, scuppers, skylights, walls, chimneys, vents, and roof edges must be carefully installed.
Wind Exposure
Homes in exposed areas can experience significant wind.

Roofing materials must be properly fastened and installed according to manufacturer requirements.
Dense Properties
Many San Francisco homes have little space between buildings.

Some properties share roof transitions or have extremely close neighboring structures.

This means contractors need to consider:

Neighboring property protection

Debris control

Material delivery

Roof access

Driveway or street access

Scaffolding

Ladders

Disposal

Protection of windows, siding, and landscaping

Proper planning is especially important before tear-off begins.
Flat Roof Replacement in San Francisco
Flat and low-slope roofing is extremely common throughout San Francisco.

These roofs require different materials and installation techniques than standard pitched shingle roofs.

One of the biggest mistakes a homeowner can make is allowing a roofing material designed for steep-slope applications to be used in an inappropriate low-slope area.
Modified Bitumen Roofing
Modified bitumen systems are commonly used on San Francisco flat and low-slope residential roofs.

Depending on the particular system, installation may include multiple layers such as:

Base sheet

Reinforced membrane

Modified bitumen roofing membrane

Flashing membrane

Cap sheet or finished roofing layer

The exact system depends on the existing building, manufacturer, roof slope, substrate, drainage design, and project requirements.
Flat Roof Drainage Is Critical
Flat roofs are not usually completely flat.

They need sufficient drainage to move rainwater toward:

Roof drains

Scuppers

Gutters

Downspouts

If the existing roof has significant ponding, the drainage condition should be evaluated before installing the new roof.

Simply installing new roofing material over an area with a major drainage problem may not correct the underlying condition.

Depending on the roof, correcting drainage may involve:

Tapered materials

Crickets

Framing modifications

New sheathing

Drain modifications

Slope improvements

Every property should be evaluated individually.
Asphalt Shingle Roof Replacement in San Francisco
Many pitched San Francisco homes use architectural asphalt shingles.

Modern architectural shingles offer homeowners numerous advantages:

Attractive appearance

Multiple colors and styles

Good weather resistance

Relatively efficient installation

Manufacturer warranty options

Compatibility with many San Francisco architectural styles

Premium shingles may also provide enhanced features such as solar-reflective technology or upgraded manufacturer warranty eligibility.

The quality of installation, however, is just as important as the shingle itself.

A premium roofing product installed over deteriorated plywood or improperly installed flashing may still develop problems.
What Is Included in a Complete Roof Replacement?
A professional San Francisco roof replacement should address the complete roofing assembly.

Here is what homeowners should expect.
1. Existing Roof Removal
Existing roofing materials are removed from the areas included in the project.

Depending on the roof, tear-off can include:

Shingles

Modified bitumen

Underlayment

Existing fasteners

Flashing

Roofing accessories

Deteriorated membranes

Removing the existing roofing allows the contractor to see what is underneath.
2. Roof Deck Inspection
Once the old roof is removed, the exposed roof deck should be inspected.

Roof sheathing may contain damage that was impossible to identify during the original exterior inspection.

Common concealed problems include:

Rotten plywood

Delamination

Dry rot

Water-damaged sheathing

Previous improper repairs

Damaged framing

Structural deficiencies

Damaged decking should be properly addressed before the new roofing system is installed.
3. Roof Deck Repairs
If deteriorated sheathing is discovered, damaged sections may need replacement.

This is one reason homeowners should ask their contractor before signing a contract:

How much does additional plywood cost if damaged decking is discovered?

A professional roofing proposal should explain how concealed damage will be handled.
4. Underlayment
Underlayment provides an additional protective layer between the roof deck and finished roofing material.

Depending on the roofing system, this may include modern synthetic roofing underlayment or another manufacturer-approved product.

Underlayment plays an important part in the complete roofing system.
5. Waterproofing Critical Areas
Additional waterproofing protection may be installed around vulnerable roof areas including:

Valleys

Roof penetrations

Skylights

Eaves

Chimneys

Roof-to-wall connections

Low-slope transitions

These are often the places where leaks develop first.
6. Flashing Installation
Flashing is one of the most important components of a roof.

Flashing directs water away from joints and transitions where roofing materials meet another surface.

San Francisco homes can have complicated flashing conditions involving:

Parapet walls

Chimneys

Skylights

Neighboring walls

Plumbing vents

HVAC penetrations

Roof-to-wall transitions

Sidewalls

Headwalls

Poor flashing installation can cause leakage even when the main roofing material remains in excellent condition.
7. New Roofing Installation
After the roof deck and waterproofing details are prepared, the new roofing system is installed according to the manufacturer's applicable installation instructions.

Depending on the property, this may include:

Architectural shingles

Modified bitumen roofing

Low-slope membranes

Combination roofing systems

8. Roof Penetrations
Every penetration through the roof needs proper integration with the roofing system.

Examples include:

Plumbing vents

Exhaust vents

Skylights

Chimneys

Roof drains

HVAC equipment

Electrical penetrations

Solar-related components

These areas should be carefully inspected during reroofing.
9. Cleanup
Roof replacement produces a significant amount of debris.

Professional cleanup should include removing roofing debris and checking work areas around the property.

Because San Francisco properties frequently have narrow side yards and neighboring buildings, debris management is especially important.
10. Final Inspection
Once construction is complete, the contractor should review the finished roofing installation.

Projects requiring a building permit must also complete the applicable City inspection process.

San Francisco's Department of Building Inspection allows reroofing inspections associated with permits to be requested through PermitSF.
Do You Need a Permit for Roof Replacement in San Francisco?
This is an important question.

Under San Francisco's current Building Code, reroofing can be exempt from a building permit when no roof sheathing is installed, repaired, or removed and the reroofed area does not exceed 25% of the entire roof surface within a 12-month period.

That means a typical full roof replacement in San Francisco generally requires a building permit.

Permit requirements can become more complicated when work involves:

Roof sheathing

Structural alterations

Historic properties

Major roof modifications

Rooftop equipment

Changes to drainage

Solar systems

Fire-safety considerations

Other exterior alterations

Certain historic buildings may also require additional Planning review when the roofing project changes the roof structure or sheathing.

Your roofing contractor should evaluate the permit requirements before beginning work.
San Francisco Cool Roof Requirements
Roof replacement in San Francisco may also involve applicable California energy-efficiency and cool roof requirements.

The exact requirements can depend on factors including:

Roof slope

Roofing area

Building type

Scope of construction

Roofing product

Applicable energy-code provisions

For applicable projects, roofing materials may need to meet specified solar reflectance and thermal emittance requirements.

Because codes change over time and different buildings can qualify for different exceptions or requirements, the roofing system should be confirmed for the particular property before installation.
Roof Replacement on Historic San Francisco Homes
San Francisco contains thousands of older and architecturally distinctive buildings.

If you own a Victorian, Edwardian, or historically significant home, roofing work may require additional planning.

A historic roof can include:

Unusual roof slopes

Decorative architectural elements

Turrets

Dormers

Multiple valleys

Custom gutters

Complex flashing

Old framing

Multiple previous roof layers

Historic properties can also be subject to additional review depending on the scope of exterior alterations.

This is another reason why homeowners should avoid assuming that every San Francisco reroof is a simple one- or two-day shingle installation.
Should You Replace Skylights During Roof Replacement?
Roof replacement is one of the best times to evaluate existing skylights.

Removing an old roof provides access to skylight flashing, curbs, surrounding framing, and decking.

Older skylights may have:

Deteriorated seals

Damaged glazing

Corroded metal

Failed flashing

Rotten curbs

Deteriorated surrounding plywood

Previous patches

Interior water staining

If a skylight is already near the end of its useful life, replacing it at the same time as the roof can be more efficient than disturbing a newly installed roofing system several years later.

San Francisco also has many custom skylights that cannot always be replaced with a standard off-the-shelf unit.

In these cases, measurements and product availability should be confirmed before the roof replacement begins.
What About Roof-to-Wall and Neighboring Roof Connections?
This issue is particularly important in San Francisco.

Homes are frequently constructed extremely close together, and some roof areas connect directly against neighboring walls or roofs.

These areas can create complicated waterproofing conditions.

A contractor should evaluate:

Existing wall flashing

Counterflashing

Siding condition

Neighboring roofing

Parapet walls

Drainage

Property access

Waterproofing transitions

When work requires access to a neighboring property, the homeowner should determine whether permission is required before construction begins.

These details should be discussed before tear-off, not after the roofing project is underway.
How Much Does Roof Replacement Cost in San Francisco?
There is no reliable single price for every San Francisco roof.

Two homes with the same roof square footage can have dramatically different project costs.

Factors affecting San Francisco roof replacement cost include:
Roof Size
More roofing area means additional labor, material, disposal, and installation time.
Roof Type
A pitched asphalt shingle roof has different installation requirements than a multi-layer low-slope roofing system.
Existing Roofing Layers
Multiple existing layers may increase tear-off and disposal costs.
Roof Access
San Francisco access conditions can greatly affect labor.

Some homes have:

No driveway

Narrow side access

Steep streets

Limited parking

Multi-story roof access

Neighboring buildings very close to the property

Roof Height
Working on a three-story San Francisco home can require substantially more safety preparation than reroofing a single-story building.
Roof Complexity
Roof cost may increase when a building contains:

Multiple skylights

Chimneys

Dormers

Valleys

Parapet walls

Roof decks

Multiple roof elevations

Difficult transitions

Plywood Damage
Decking deterioration usually cannot be fully identified until tear-off.

Extensive dry rot or damaged framing can increase the scope of work.
Roofing Materials
Different materials have different costs.

Standard architectural shingles and premium shingles do not cost the same.

Likewise, a multi-layer modified bitumen system has different material and labor requirements than shingles.
Permits
Applicable City permit and inspection requirements should also be considered.

The most accurate way to determine your roof replacement price is through an on-site roof inspection followed by a detailed written proposal.
How Long Does Roof Replacement Take in San Francisco?
A typical residential roof replacement may take several working days, but there is no universal timeline.

Project length depends on:

Roof size

Roof height

Roofing system

Roof complexity

Existing roofing layers

Access

Decking repairs

Skylights

Weather

Structural repairs

Permit requirements

Required inspections

A simple roof can progress relatively quickly.

A complicated multi-story San Francisco property with multiple skylights, flat roof sections, parapets, and significant plywood replacement can take considerably longer.
What Happens if It Rains During Roof Replacement?
Weather monitoring is an important part of roofing operations.

Contractors should avoid exposing more of the roof than can be properly protected when rain is expected.

San Francisco roofing schedules may change during periods of wet weather.

Homeowners should understand that a weather-related schedule adjustment is often made to protect the property rather than simply to delay the project.
Roof Repair vs. Full Roof Replacement
Sometimes a roof repair is enough.
Roof Repair May Make Sense When:

The roof is relatively new

Damage is isolated

Only one flashing area has failed

Only a few shingles are damaged

Most of the roofing system remains in good condition

Roof Replacement May Make More Sense When:

The roof has recurring leaks

Roofing is deteriorated throughout

Numerous previous repairs are visible

The roof is approaching the end of its expected service life

Multiple areas are leaking

Significant membrane deterioration exists

Roof decking has widespread damage

Repair expenses continue increasing

A professional contractor should explain your options rather than automatically recommending complete replacement.
Questions to Ask a San Francisco Roofing Contractor
Before hiring a roofing contractor, ask detailed questions.
Is the Contractor Licensed?
Verify that your contractor holds the appropriate California contractor license.
Is the Contractor Insured?
Ask about applicable workers' compensation and general liability insurance.
What Roofing System Will Be Installed?
The proposal should identify the roofing system and important materials.
Does the Price Include Tear-Off?
Do not assume.

Make sure removal and disposal are clearly stated.
What Happens if Rotten Plywood Is Found?
Understand additional decking pricing before construction begins.
Who Handles the Permit?
Determine whether the contractor will obtain and coordinate the required roofing permit and inspections.
What Is the Workmanship Warranty?
Ask exactly how long installation workmanship is covered.
What Manufacturer Warranty Is Included?
Manufacturer warranties and contractor workmanship warranties are different.

Ask for both.
What Is Excluded?
A professional contract should clearly identify exclusions.
Don't Compare Roofing Estimates Based Only on Price
Roofing proposals can appear similar while including very different scopes of work.

For example, one proposal might include:

Complete tear-off

Premium underlayment

Waterproofing

New flashing

Vent replacement

Permit coordination

Deck inspection

Disposal

Manufacturer warranty

Another quote may only state:

“Remove existing roof and install new roof.”

Those are not necessarily equivalent proposals.

Before choosing a contractor, compare:

Materials

Roof system

Underlayment

Flashing

Decking terms

Ventilation

Skylights

Permit

Disposal

Warranty

Cleanup

Exclusions

The lowest initial price is not always the lowest long-term roofing cost.
San Francisco Neighborhoods We Serve
Roof Express provides roofing services throughout San Francisco, including:

Sunset District

Outer Sunset

Inner Sunset

Richmond District

Outer Richmond

Inner Richmond

Noe Valley

Bernal Heights

Glen Park

Excelsior

Mission District

Marina District

Pacific Heights

Potrero Hill

Russian Hill

Nob Hill

Twin Peaks

West Portal

Ingleside

Visitacion Valley

Bayview

Hunters Point

Haight-Ashbury

Cole Valley

Castro District

Diamond Heights

Presidio Heights

North Beach

SOMA

Oceanview

Crocker-Amazon

Every neighborhood has different building types, exposure conditions, access challenges, and roofing designs.

An on-site evaluation remains the best way to recommend the correct roofing system.
How to Prepare Your Home for Roof Replacement
Before construction begins, homeowners can make the process easier by preparing the property.

Consider:

Moving vehicles away from the work area

Providing clear property access

Moving patio furniture

Protecting fragile landscaping

Removing fragile wall decorations

Protecting items stored in the attic

Keeping pets and children away from work zones

Informing tenants about construction

Providing gate access where required

Discussing neighbor access in advance

Identifying rooftop equipment

Discussing skylights before material ordering

Identifying solar equipment

Roof replacement creates vibration, noise, and debris.

Preparing before construction helps reduce surprises.
Why the Complete Roofing System Matters
A roof is much more than the material visible from the street.

A complete roofing system includes:

Roof deck → waterproofing → underlayment → flashing → finished roofing → penetrations → ventilation → drainage

Every part must work together.

A premium roofing membrane cannot compensate for severely deteriorated decking.

Expensive shingles cannot stop water entering through incorrectly installed flashing.

And a new flat roof may continue experiencing problems if significant drainage conditions are ignored.

The quality of both the roofing system and the installation matters.
Why Choose Roof Express for Roof Replacement in San Francisco?
When you're investing in a new roof, you need a contractor who understands San Francisco properties.

Roof Express provides professional roof inspections, roof replacement, flat roofing, asphalt shingle roofing, skylight replacement, flashing work, waterproofing, roof decking replacement, gutters, and other roofing services throughout San Francisco and the Bay Area.

We work with both pitched and low-slope roofing systems and understand the challenges associated with San Francisco's older buildings, tight access, complicated roof transitions, skylights, attached structures, and flat roofs.

Roof Express operates under General Express Construction DBA Roof Express, California CSLB License No. 1072766.
Schedule a Roof Replacement Estimate in San Francisco
If your roof is leaking, deteriorating, or approaching the end of its expected life, don't wait until minor roofing problems cause major interior damage.

Schedule a professional roof inspection with Roof Express.

We can evaluate your:

Existing roofing

Roof deck

Flashing

Skylights

Flat roof sections

Roof drainage

Penetrations

Gutters

Ventilation

Visible problem areas

After the inspection, we can provide a detailed roofing proposal based on your property's actual conditions.

Looking for a reliable roof replacement contractor in San Francisco, CA? Contact Roof Express today to schedule your roof inspection and request an estimate.
Frequently Asked Questions About Roof Replacement in San FranciscoDo I need a permit to replace my roof in San Francisco?
A typical complete reroof generally requires a building permit. Under the San Francisco Building Code, limited reroofing not exceeding 25% of the roof surface within a 12-month period can qualify for a permit exemption when no roof sheathing is installed, repaired, or removed.
What type of roof is best for San Francisco?
It depends on the building and roof slope. Architectural asphalt shingles are commonly used on pitched roofs, while modified bitumen and other low-slope systems are commonly used on flat and low-slope roofs.
How much does a new roof cost in San Francisco?
Pricing depends on roof size, roofing material, height, access, complexity, number of existing layers, decking condition, skylights, flashing, permits, and other project conditions. An on-site inspection is the best way to obtain accurate pricing.
How long does a roof replacement take?
Many residential roofing projects can be completed within several working days. Large or complicated properties, substantial dry rot, weather delays, specialty materials, skylights, or structural repairs may extend the schedule.
Can you replace a flat roof in San Francisco?
Yes. Flat and low-slope roofing is common in San Francisco. The correct roofing system should be selected based on roof slope, drainage, existing conditions, and building requirements.
Should I replace my skylights when replacing my roof?
Older skylights should be evaluated during reroofing. If a skylight is already deteriorated or approaching the end of its useful life, replacing it during roof construction may be more practical than disturbing a new roof later.
Can you install a new roof over my existing roof?
Whether an overlay is appropriate depends on existing roofing layers, roof conditions, applicable codes, manufacturer requirements, weight, drainage, and the roofing system being installed. Complete tear-off also allows the roof deck to be inspected.
What happens if rotten plywood is discovered?
Deteriorated decking should be replaced as necessary to provide a suitable substrate for the roofing system. Your contract should explain how additional decking replacement will be priced and approved.
Does San Francisco require roof inspections after replacement?
Permitted projects are subject to applicable City inspection requirements. San Francisco DBI currently allows reroofing inspections for PermitSF-issued permits to be requested through the PermitSF dashboard.
Can Roof Express work on both shingles and flat roofing?
Yes. Roof Express performs pitched shingle roofing as well as flat and low-slope roofing systems, allowing combination-roof properties to be evaluated as a complete roofing system.
How do I get a roof replacement estimate?
Contact Roof Express to schedule a roof inspection. We will inspect the visible roof conditions and provide a written proposal based on the recommended scope of work.

Flat Roof Replacement in San FranciscoComplete Homeowner Guide
Flat and low-slope roofs are a major part of San Francisco's residential architecture.

From the Sunset and Richmond districts to Noe Valley, Bernal Heights, Mission, Excelsior, Potrero Hill, and other neighborhoods, thousands of San Francisco homes have flat or low-slope roofing systems.

These roofs require a very different approach from conventional pitched shingle roofs.

When a flat roof begins leaking, developing open seams, showing bubbles or blisters, holding excessive water, or requiring repeated repairs, it may be time to consider a complete flat roof replacement in San Francisco.

At Roof Express, we provide professional flat and low-slope roofing services throughout San Francisco and the Bay Area, including modified bitumen roofing, multi-layer torch-down systems, roof-deck replacement, skylight work, flashing, drainage improvements, and complete reroofing.

This guide explains what San Francisco property owners should know before replacing a flat roof.
Why Flat Roofs Are So Common in San Francisco
San Francisco has a unique collection of homes and multi-unit residential buildings.

Many buildings are constructed on narrow lots where a flat or low-slope roof allows homeowners to maximize interior space while maintaining the building's architectural profile.

Flat roofs are common on:

Victorian and Edwardian properties

Row houses

Multi-unit buildings

Residential additions

Garages

Modern homes

Mixed pitched-and-flat roof structures

Many San Francisco roofs also contain additional components such as:

Skylights

Roof drains

Scuppers

Parapet walls

Chimneys

Plumbing vents

Solar equipment

HVAC equipment

Roof decks

Light wells

Neighboring roof-to-wall connections

Each of these areas requires proper waterproofing.
When Should a San Francisco Flat Roof Be Replaced?
Not every roof leak means you need a complete roof replacement.

If a relatively new roofing system has one isolated flashing problem, repair may be sufficient.

However, replacement becomes more practical when deterioration affects the roofing system as a whole.

Common warning signs include:

Recurring roof leaks

Open or deteriorated seams

Cracking roofing membranes

Large bubbles or blisters

Multiple patched areas

Exposed or deteriorated roofing material

Soft roof decking

Water damage underneath the membrane

Failed roof-to-wall flashing

Deteriorated parapet flashing

Leaking skylights

Deterioration around drains

Persistent ponding water

Interior ceiling stains

Roofing approaching the end of its expected service life

If you're repairing the roof every rainy season, a complete replacement may provide better long-term value than continuing to patch an aging system.
What Is the Best Flat Roofing System for San Francisco?
There is no single roofing system that is correct for every building.

The right system depends on:

Roof slope

Existing roofing

Roof decking

Drainage

Building construction

Parapets

Skylights

Roof penetrations

Fire-safety requirements

Manufacturer specifications

Building-code requirements

One of the systems commonly used for residential low-slope roofing is modified bitumen roofing.
Modified Bitumen Flat Roofing
Modified bitumen is an asphalt-based roofing membrane specifically designed for low-slope applications.

Unlike conventional shingles, which depend heavily on roof slope to shed water, a modified bitumen roofing assembly is designed to provide continuous waterproof protection.

A properly installed modified bitumen system can provide:

Multiple waterproofing layers

Reinforced membranes

Strong seam protection

Durable surface protection

Effective detailing around penetrations

Compatibility with many San Francisco flat roofs

Modified bitumen is available in several systems and installation methods.

One option is a multi-layer torch-applied system.
3-Layer Torch-Down Roofing in San Francisco
For appropriate properties, Roof Express may recommend a 3-layer modified bitumen roofing system.

A typical multi-ply system can consist of:

Layer 1 – Base Sheet

Layer 2 – Modified Bitumen Interply

Layer 3 – Granulated Modified Bitumen Cap Sheet

These layers work together to create a reinforced roofing assembly.

Instead of depending on one surface membrane, the roofing system provides multiple layers of waterproofing protection.

This type of construction can be especially beneficial on low-slope roofs where water moves more slowly than it does on a steep shingle roof.
How Torch-Down Roofing Works
Torch-applied modified bitumen uses controlled heat during installation to bond compatible roofing membranes to the approved substrate or underlying roofing layer.

When installed correctly, the process creates bonded seams and a continuous waterproofing system.

Because torch-down roofing involves hot work and open-flame equipment, additional safety requirements can apply.

San Francisco's Department of Building Inspection guidance specifically notes that roofing involving hot work, including torch-down work, is routed to the San Francisco Fire Department as part of applicable permitting review.

This is one reason torch-applied roofing should be performed only by qualified roofing professionals using appropriate equipment and safety procedures.
Complete Flat Roof Replacement Process
A professional flat roof replacement involves much more than installing a new membrane over the existing roof.

Here is how a complete project may be approached.
1. Detailed Roof Inspection
Before construction begins, the roofing contractor should inspect the entire roof.

Important conditions include:

Existing membrane

Seams

Roof edges

Parapet walls

Skylights

Drains

Scuppers

Plumbing vents

Roof-to-wall connections

Low areas

Existing patches

Visible decking problems

The purpose of the inspection is to determine whether repair, overlay, or complete tear-off is the most appropriate approach.
2. Removal of the Existing Roofing
For a complete replacement, the existing roofing material is removed from the areas included in the project.

Tear-off may include:

Existing roofing membranes

Old cap sheets

Base materials

Loose flashing

Fasteners

Previous patching materials

Deteriorated roofing accessories

Removing the old system allows the contractor to see the condition underneath.
3. Roof Deck Inspection
One of the biggest advantages of a complete tear-off is that it exposes the roof decking.

Concealed damage may include:

Rotten plywood

Soft decking

Water damage

Delamination

Dry rot

Previous improper repairs

Damaged framing

A new flat roof should be installed over a sound and properly prepared substrate.

Covering severe decking deterioration with another roofing membrane does not correct the underlying problem.
4. Roof Deck Replacement
Deteriorated plywood or sheathing should be replaced where necessary before the new roofing system is installed.

Homeowners should understand how decking replacement will be handled before signing a roofing contract.

A detailed proposal should explain:

Any included plywood allowance

Additional decking cost

How concealed conditions are documented

How additional work is authorized

Structural repairs that may be excluded

Clear terms can prevent surprises during construction.
5. Evaluate Roof Slope and Drainage
Drainage is one of the most important parts of a San Francisco flat roof.

Despite the name, a properly functioning "flat" roof should generally have enough slope to direct water toward the intended drainage system.

Water may drain toward:

Roof drains

Scuppers

Gutters

Downspouts

If the existing roof has significant ponding, installing a new membrane alone does not necessarily fix the slope.

Depending on existing conditions, drainage improvements may require:

Tapered roofing materials

Crickets

Framing modifications

New plywood

Drain modifications

Scupper improvements

Other slope corrections

The drainage condition should be evaluated before installation whenever practical.
Why Ponding Water Matters
Some temporary water can remain on certain low-slope roofs following rain.

However, significant or persistent ponding deserves investigation.

Ponding can occur because of:

Insufficient slope

Blocked drains

Settling

Deflected framing

Poorly positioned drains

Improper previous roof construction

Standing water can place additional stress on roofing materials and expose weak seams or flashing details.

A flat roof replacement proposal should clearly state whether drainage or slope correction is included.
6. Install the Base Sheet
Once the deck and substrate have been properly prepared, installation of the roofing system begins.

For a three-layer modified bitumen system, the first layer is typically the base sheet.

The base sheet creates a foundation for subsequent waterproofing membranes.

Its exact type and attachment depend on:

Manufacturer requirements

Roof substrate

Building conditions

Selected roofing assembly

Proper preparation at this stage is critical because every layer above depends on the foundation underneath.
7. Install the Modified Bitumen Interply
The second layer provides another reinforced waterproofing membrane.

This intermediate roofing layer increases redundancy within the system.

Rather than relying entirely on the finished cap sheet, the roof contains another continuous layer beneath it.

This is one of the primary advantages of a multi-ply roofing assembly.
8. Install the Granulated Cap Sheet
The third and final layer is commonly a granulated modified bitumen cap sheet.

This becomes the visible surface of the completed roof.

The cap sheet provides the final waterproofing layer while its granulated surface helps protect the roofing membrane from weather exposure.

The cap sheet must be properly incorporated into all important roof details.

These include:

Parapet walls

Roof drains

Scuppers

Skylights

Plumbing vents

Chimneys

Roof edges

Roof-to-wall transitions

Other penetrations

Parapet Walls and San Francisco Flat Roofs
Parapet walls are extremely common on San Francisco buildings.

They create some of the most important waterproofing transitions on a flat roof.

Water can enter where:

Roofing meets the parapet

Wall flashing deteriorates

Coping becomes loose

Old sealant fails

Previous roofing layers terminate incorrectly

During replacement, parapet conditions should be carefully evaluated.

Depending on the existing construction and scope, work may involve:

Membrane flashing

Wall flashing

Counterflashing

Coping

Waterproofing at corners

Integration with siding or stucco

Poor parapet details can cause leaks even when the main roofing membrane is in excellent condition.
Roof-to-Wall Connections
San Francisco homes are frequently built extremely close together.

In some locations, a property's flat roof terminates against another wall or neighboring structure.

These transitions require special attention.

A roofing contractor should evaluate:

Existing flashing

Wall condition

Siding

Stucco

Neighboring roofing

Counterflashing

Waterproof membrane height

Drainage path

When access to a neighboring property is necessary, property owners may need to coordinate permission before construction begins.
Flat Roof Skylights
Skylights are another common feature on San Francisco flat roofs.

During roof replacement, existing skylights should be carefully evaluated.

Problems can include:

Failed seals

Deteriorated flashing

Cracked glazing

Rotten wood

Damaged curbs

Corrosion

Old roofing cement

Interior water staining

If an aging skylight needs replacement soon, reroofing is often an ideal time to address it.

Replacing the skylight during the roofing project allows the new roof and new flashing system to be integrated together.
Custom Skylights in San Francisco
Many older San Francisco homes contain skylights that are not standard modern sizes.

These may require custom fabrication.

If custom skylights are being replaced, they should be measured and ordered before the roofing schedule is finalized whenever possible.

That can reduce unnecessary delays and avoid installing a new roof only to disturb it again when the replacement skylight arrives.
Roof Drains and Scuppers
Drainage components should never be overlooked during flat roof replacement.

Roof drains and scuppers should be checked for:

Blockages

Deteriorated flashing

Corrosion

Poor transitions

Improper height

Water buildup

Existing repairs

The roofing membrane must be properly integrated into the drainage system.

Simply applying roofing cement around an old drain is not equivalent to properly rebuilding the drainage detail when deterioration is present.
Plumbing Vents and Other Penetrations
Every hole through a roofing system creates another potential leak location.

Common San Francisco flat-roof penetrations include:

Plumbing vents

Exhaust pipes

Electrical conduits

HVAC equipment

Skylights

Chimneys

Solar mounts

Roof drains

Each penetration must be properly flashed and waterproofed as part of the new roofing system.
Solar Panels on Flat Roofs
Many San Francisco homes have rooftop solar equipment.

If panels or mounting systems interfere with the roofing work, they may need to be removed and reinstalled by the appropriate solar contractor.

This should be coordinated before tear-off begins.

The roofing contractor should also evaluate existing penetrations around solar mounts so the new waterproofing can be properly integrated.
Roof Decks Over Flat Roofs
Some San Francisco properties have decks or walking surfaces installed over roofing membranes.

These require additional planning.

The roofing contractor needs access to the waterproofing system underneath the deck.

Important considerations may include:

Deck removal

Pedestal systems

Waterproofing

Drainage

Door clearances

Guardrails

Deck penetrations

A roof deck can conceal deterioration for years, making inspection especially important when leakage occurs below it.
Do You Need a Permit for Flat Roof Replacement in San Francisco?
A complete flat roof replacement will generally require a building permit.

Under San Francisco's current Building Code, reroofing is exempt from a building permit only when no roof sheathing is installed, repaired, or removed and the reroofed area during a 12-month period does not exceed 25% of the total roof surface.

Because a complete flat roof replacement normally involves substantially more than 25% of the roof, homeowners should expect permit requirements to apply.

Additional review may also apply depending on the particular property and scope.

For example, City guidance identifies additional considerations involving historic buildings, street-space use, and hot-work roofing.
San Francisco Roof Inspections
Permitted roofing work also needs to complete applicable inspections.

San Francisco's Department of Building Inspection currently allows reroofing inspections for permits issued through PermitSF to be requested online through the applicant's PermitSF dashboard.

A professional roofing contractor should coordinate the applicable permit and inspection process as agreed in the roofing contract.
Cool Roof Requirements
Depending on the building, roofing area, project scope, roof slope, and applicable California energy standards, a flat roof replacement may also be subject to cool-roof requirements.

These rules can affect the solar reflectance and thermal characteristics of the roofing material selected.

Because applicable energy standards and exceptions can vary by project, product compliance should be verified before materials are ordered.

A roofing product should not be chosen based solely on color or appearance.
How Much Does Flat Roof Replacement Cost in San Francisco?
There is no single price that accurately represents every San Francisco flat roof.

Several factors can dramatically affect cost.
Roof Size
Larger roofs require more roofing materials, labor, tear-off, and disposal.
Number of Existing Layers
Many older San Francisco buildings have multiple generations of roofing material.

Removing several existing layers can significantly increase labor and debris disposal.
Roof Access
Access can have a major effect on San Francisco roofing costs.

Some properties have:

No driveway

Narrow side passages

Steep streets

Limited parking

Three- or four-story roof access

Buildings directly against neighboring properties

Material delivery and debris removal must be carefully planned.
Decking Condition
If significant plywood deterioration is discovered after tear-off, additional work may be required.
Number of Skylights
Flat roofs with multiple skylights require additional flashing and waterproofing work.
Parapets
Complex parapet walls and roof-to-wall transitions can increase labor.
Drainage
Projects requiring new drains, scuppers, crickets, tapered materials, or slope correction require additional work.
Roofing System
A multi-layer modified bitumen system has different labor and material requirements than a single-ply or other low-slope roofing assembly.
Roof Height
Multi-story buildings require additional safety equipment and labor.

The best way to determine the actual cost is through an on-site inspection and detailed written proposal.
How Long Does a Flat Roof Replacement Take?
Many residential flat roofs can be replaced within several working days.

However, timing depends on:

Roof size

Number of roofing layers

Height

Access

Decking repairs

Skylights

Parapet walls

Drainage corrections

Weather

Permit inspections

Roofing system

A simple garage roof is very different from a three-story San Francisco residence with multiple skylights, parapets, drains, and several old roofing layers.
What Happens if It Rains During the Project?
Weather planning is especially important during a flat roof tear-off.

A professional roofing contractor should monitor the forecast and avoid unnecessarily exposing sections of roof when rain is expected.

Roofing work may occasionally be postponed because of weather.

Although schedule changes can be inconvenient, preventing water from entering an exposed building should be the priority.
Repair or Replace Your San Francisco Flat Roof?
A repair may be appropriate when:

The roofing system is relatively new

Damage is localized

One flashing detail has failed

One penetration is leaking

The surrounding membrane remains in good condition

Complete replacement may be more practical when:

Multiple areas are leaking

Membranes are deteriorated throughout

Many repairs already exist

Roofing seams are failing

Roof decking is damaged

The roof is reaching the end of its expected service life

Annual repair costs continue increasing

A reputable roofing contractor should explain both options when repair remains realistic.
Avoid Repeated Temporary Patching
Roofing cement and temporary sealants can be useful in certain repair situations.

However, continuously applying additional material over an old failing roof does not restore the original roofing system.

Eventually, layers of previous repairs can:

Hide the original problem

Trap moisture

Make future repairs more difficult

Increase tear-off labor

Create uneven surfaces

When deterioration becomes widespread, replacement can provide a cleaner long-term solution.
Benefits of a Complete Flat Roof Replacement
A properly designed replacement can provide several advantages.
New Waterproofing System
Old and deteriorated membranes are replaced with a complete new roofing assembly.
Roof Deck Inspection
Tear-off allows concealed plywood damage to be identified.
New Flashing
Problematic roof transitions can be rebuilt and integrated into the new roof.
Improved Drainage Opportunities
Existing ponding or drainage problems can be evaluated before the finished membrane is installed.
Skylight Integration
Older skylights and curbs can be replaced or reflashed as part of the roofing project.
Cleaner Finished Appearance
A complete replacement eliminates years of visible patchwork and provides a uniform finished roof surface.
Maintaining a New Flat Roof
A flat roof should be inspected and maintained even after replacement.

Homeowners should periodically:

Keep roof drains clear

Remove leaves and debris

Check scuppers

Inspect skylights

Monitor roof penetrations

Check flashing

Avoid unnecessary foot traffic

Inspect after major storms

Have roof work coordinated when solar, HVAC, electrical, or plumbing contractors need rooftop access

Other trades can accidentally damage roofing membranes while installing equipment.

Any new penetration should be coordinated with a qualified roofing contractor.
San Francisco Neighborhoods We Serve
Roof Express provides flat roofing services throughout San Francisco, including:

Sunset District

Outer Sunset

Inner Sunset

Richmond District

Outer Richmond

Inner Richmond

West Portal

Noe Valley

Excelsior

Ingleside

Mission District

Potrero Hill

Bayview

Marina District

Pacific Heights

Russian Hill

Nob Hill

Twin Peaks

Diamond Heights

Castro

Haight-Ashbury

Cole Valley

North Beach

Visitacion Valley

Crocker-Amazon

Every roof has different construction, access, drainage, and waterproofing requirements.

An on-site inspection is therefore important before recommending a particular roofing system.
Choosing a San Francisco Flat Roofing Contractor
Before hiring a contractor, homeowners should ask detailed questions.

Make sure the proposal identifies:

Roofing system

Number of roofing layers

Tear-off

Disposal

Decking terms

Base sheet

Membranes

Cap sheet

Flashing

Parapet work

Drain work

Skylights

Permit handling

Cleanup

Manufacturer warranty

Workmanship warranty

Exclusions

Also confirm appropriate California contractor licensing and applicable insurance coverage.

Do not select a flat roofing contractor based only on the lowest total price.

Two roofing proposals can have dramatically different scopes even when both say "new flat roof."
Why Choose Roof Express for Flat Roof Replacement in San Francisco?
Roof Express provides professional residential roofing services throughout San Francisco and the greater Bay Area.

Our flat roofing services include:

Complete flat roof replacement

Modified bitumen roofing

Multi-layer torch-down roofing

Low-slope roofing

Roof repair

Roof-deck replacement

Skylight replacement

Parapet waterproofing

Roof-to-wall flashing

Roof drain and scupper work

Drainage improvements

Gutters and downspouts

Roof inspections

Preventive maintenance

We evaluate more than just the visible roofing surface.

Our goal is to address the complete roof assembly — including the substrate, waterproofing, flashing, penetrations, drainage, and finished roofing system.

Roof Express operates under General Express Construction DBA Roof Express, California CSLB License No. 1072766.
Schedule Your San Francisco Flat Roof Inspection
If your flat roof is leaking, holding water, developing bubbles, showing open seams, or requiring frequent repairs, schedule a professional inspection before the problem causes additional damage.

Roof Express can evaluate:

Existing roofing membranes

Roof decking

Parapets

Flashing

Skylights

Drains

Scuppers

Roof penetrations

Drainage

Ponding areas

Existing repairs

We can then provide a detailed written proposal based on the actual conditions of your property.

Looking for a flat roof replacement contractor in San Francisco, CA? Contact Roof Express today to schedule your roof inspection and request an estimate.
Frequently Asked Questions About Flat Roof Replacement in San FranciscoWhat is the best roofing system for a San Francisco flat roof?
The best system depends on roof slope, existing construction, drainage, roof deck, penetrations, building requirements, and budget. Modified bitumen is one commonly used low-slope roofing option.
Is a 3-layer torch-down roof a good option?
A properly designed multi-ply modified bitumen system can provide strong waterproofing redundancy for appropriate low-slope applications. The exact system should be selected according to manufacturer instructions, building conditions, and applicable requirements.
Do I need a permit to replace my flat roof in San Francisco?
A complete reroof generally requires a permit. The current San Francisco Building Code exempts reroofing only when no roof sheathing is installed, repaired, or removed and the work does not exceed 25% of the total roof surface within a 12-month period.
Does torch-down roofing require special consideration in San Francisco?
Yes. San Francisco DBI guidance identifies torch-down roofing as hot work and notes routing to the San Francisco Fire Department where applicable.
Can a new flat roof eliminate ponding water?
Not automatically. A new roofing membrane provides waterproofing but does not necessarily change the existing roof slope. Significant ponding may require separate drainage or slope improvements.
Should I replace my skylights while replacing my flat roof?
Older or deteriorated skylights should be evaluated during reroofing. Replacing them at the same time can allow the new skylight and roof flashing to be integrated into the new roofing system.
What happens if rotten plywood is found?
Deteriorated roof decking should be addressed before installation of the new roof. Your roofing contract should explain how concealed decking repairs will be priced and approved.
Can you install a new flat roof over an existing roof?
An overlay may be possible in certain situations, but existing layers, moisture, decking condition, weight, applicable code requirements, and roofing manufacturer requirements must first be evaluated.
How long does flat roof replacement take?
Many residential projects take several working days. Large roofs, difficult access, multiple existing layers, decking repairs, skylights, drainage work, weather, and inspections can extend the schedule.
Does a new flat roof require maintenance?
Yes. Drains and scuppers should remain clear, and roofing membranes, penetrations, flashing, skylights, and other components should be periodically inspected.
How do I get a flat roof replacement estimate in San Francisco?
Contact Roof Express to schedule an inspection. After evaluating the existing roof and its drainage, decking, flashing, penetrations, and access conditions, we can provide a detailed written proposal.
